title: Section 3
context: A student, Mia, is discussing her dissertation on renewable energy with her supervisor, Dr Patel.

audio.t: You will hear a student called Mia talking to her supervisor, Dr Patel, about her dissertation on renewable energy.
Come in, Mia. Let's see how your dissertation is coming along.
Thanks, Dr Patel. I've done a lot since our last meeting, but I'd like your advice on a few things.
Of course. Before we start, remind me how you came to choose renewable energy. Was it the documentary you mentioned in the first term?
The documentary made me curious, yes, but what really decided it was my work placement at an energy company last summer.
I saw how difficult it is to persuade local people to accept new projects, and I wanted to understand that better.
That's a good reason. Now, last time you were planning to study household solar panels. Is that still your focus?
No, I changed my mind. You said it was too broad, so I've narrowed it down to community-owned wind projects in rural areas.
Excellent, that's far more manageable. So what has been the hardest part so far?
I thought finding published research would be a problem, but there's plenty available. The real difficulty has been getting people to answer my questionnaire.
I've sent it to two hundred households, and only thirty-five have replied.
That's quite common, I'm afraid. How many responses do you think you need?
I was hoping for eighty, to make the statistics more reliable.
Eighty would be ideal, but it isn't realistic with your deadline. I'd say fifty is enough for a project of this size.
That's a relief. I'll send a reminder to the households that haven't replied yet.
Good. Have you completed the ethics form for the questionnaire?
Yes, that was approved two weeks ago.
Then the next step is to book an appointment with the statistics adviser, so she can check your analysis plan before you start.
OK, I'll do that this week. Could we look at the chapters now? I've written a first draft of all of them.
Certainly. Let's begin with the introduction. It runs to nearly two thousand words, which is much too long.
I wanted to give plenty of background on climate policy.
I understand, but you could cut it by half. The reader needs your research question quickly.
All right. And what about the literature review?
It's well organised, but most of your sources are from before 2015. This field changes fast, so you should add some more recent studies.
I'll look for papers from the last three years, then. What about the methodology chapter?
The description is clear, but the full questionnaire takes up three pages in the middle of the chapter. I'd move it to an appendix.
Would it help to add some interviews with local residents as well?
It would be interesting, but you simply don't have time. Please concentrate on the questionnaire data.
Fine. In the results chapter, I've described all the figures in paragraphs. Is that a problem?
It's hard to follow. I'd present the main figures in a chart, which will make the patterns clearer.
Good idea. And finally, the conclusion?
That's where I had most difficulty. It's a good summary, but your own argument isn't clear, so make it clearer what you are claiming.
I see. I'll rewrite it once I've finished the other chapters. Thank you so much, Dr Patel.
You're welcome, Mia. Email me the revised draft when it's ready, and good luck with the questionnaires.
